evidence_quotes.quote: Five short case studies of water insecurity demonstrate how neo-liberalism props up and legitimises decentralised water governance in Canada, which in turn promotes and maintains environmental inequality, Indigenous marginalisation and, ultimately, the Canadian identity.
In this article I argue that Indigenous exclusion, an outgrowth of the settler myths that are woven into Canadian identity, is the bedrock factor in maintaining Indigenous water insecurity.
In fact, 28 per cent of houses on First Nations reserves lack piped water with 13.5 per cent using truck delivery (Statistics Canada 2012).
A sample of case studies demonstrates the variety of water insecurity experiences across Indigenous Canada; two Inuit and three First Nations communities are featured.
It is important to note that the Strategy included reserves only; non-status First Nations, Inuit, and Métis communities were excluded.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community drinking water and wastewater service access disparities in Indigenous (First Nations, Inuit, and Métis) communities in Canada, including lack of piped water, reliance on trucked water or potable water dispensing units, and unmonitored surface water retrieval.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: YES — discusses decentralised water governance in Canada, federal/provincial jurisdiction, constitutional provisions (Sections 35 and 36), the 2012 Safe Drinking Water for First Nations Act, reserve-only eligibility under federal water programmes, and community cost-sharing expectations. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: NO — the paper's actual explanatory focus is unanalysed macro-governance and ideological background (Canadian national identity, settler myths, colonialism, and neo-liberal decentralisation). Although rule-adjacent features (reserve-only programme boundaries excluding Inuit and Métis communities, irregular provincial funding of a potable dispensing unit, and 20 per cent community cost-sharing expectations) are mentioned briefly in passing, none is empirically analysed as a rule-type mechanism governing service access. Note that even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the overall decision remains exclude because the paper lacks empirical evidence (E05).
criterion_notes.c3: NO — this is a theoretical/policy commentary essay with no empirical methodology, no primary quantitative or qualitative data collection, no original socio-legal empirical analysis, and no systematic review protocol. The five 'short case studies' (one short paragraph each on Rigolet, Black Tickle-Domino, Dokis First Nation, Kashechewan First Nation, and Walpole Island First Nation) are purely illustrative secondary summaries drawn from previously published studies and a newspaper report.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports secondary statistics and illustrative vignettes relevant to drinking water and wastewater access, piped connection disparities, boil-water advisories, potable water dispensing unit breakdowns, and water quality/quantity insecurity.
criterion_notes.c5: NO — while the broad population (Indigenous peoples and communities in Canada) and secondary water insecurity indicators are described, there is no identifiable empirical study design, sample, or operationalised exposure-outcome analysis.
criterion_notes.c6: Published in English (with a bilingual English/French abstract).

study_design: Theoretical/policy commentary essay with brief narrative secondary vignettes (non-empirical)
population_and_sample: Indigenous peoples and communities in Canada (First Nations, Inuit, and Métis), illustrated via secondary statistics and five single-paragraph secondary vignettes (no primary empirical sample)
exposure: Canadian national identity, ongoing settler colonialism, neo-liberal ideology, and decentralised water governance (theoretical/commentary framing)
outcome: Secondary national statistics and illustrative community vignettes on lack of piped water and wastewater connections, reliance on truck delivery or potable water dispensing units, boil-water advisories, and source-water contamination
rationale: Exclude under E05 (No empirical evidence). Full text matches record metadata (Hanrahan 2017, British Journal of Canadian Studies). Although the article addresses Indigenous drinking water and wastewater service access disparities in Canada (c1=yes, c4=yes), it is a theoretical and policy commentary arguing that Canadian national identity, settler colonialism, and neo-liberal decentralised governance maintain Indigenous water insecurity. It presents no empirical methods, no primary data, and no systematic synthesis—its five 'short case studies' are single-paragraph secondary summaries of prior publications and a news article (c3=no, c5=no). In addition, while it passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 by discussing water governance and statutory/programme frameworks, its analytical focus is macro-ideological governance background rather than empirical analysis of a rule-type access mechanism under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading (c2=no). Because c3 fails, both decision and plain_criterion2_decision are exclude.
